parts.required: 1.2 Compare and contrast the performance of Bank A versus its competitor over the three years. Where has Bank A excelled and where has it underperformed? Motivate your answer using appropriate ratios and analysis of the financials.
parts.memo:
The focus here is on ROA and ROE (given that NIM was already covered above).

  |  2025  |  2024  |  2023
ROA  |  0,75%  |  0,82%  |  0,91%
ROE  |  9,2%  |  9,7%  |  10,3%
  Profit Margin  |  46,7%  |  45,3%  |  43,0%
  Asset Utilization  |  0,016  |  0,018  |  0,021
  Equity Multiplier  |  12,24  |  11,84  |  11,27

1 marks per calculation (15 marks total)

ROA has been declining steadily over time. This is consistent with the same trend in the ROA of Bank B but Bank A’s ROA is slightly higher over the three years. The drivers are a combination of the profits being flat (growth of only 0,8% in 2024 and 0,5% in 2025) and total assets growing significantly faster over the same period (12,8% in 2024 and 9,2% in 2025), This is worrying because we would expect the bank’s profits to at least keep pace with its asset growth but this has not been the case. This suggests that either the bank’s revenue is not growing fast enough, or that its growth in costs are outpacing its revenue, or its mix of earning assets is not yielding the revenue it would expect.

Breaking this down, we see that Bank A’s profit margin has been increasing steadily over the period while its asset utilization has been decreasing. The increasing profit margin is interesting as the bank’s operating income has been declining over the period indicating lower revenue-generation. Despite this, the bank’s profits have increased slightly over the same time. This is largely a function of the bank’s significant decreases in credit impairments over the three years, although it has managed some control of its costs with operating expenses decreasing in 2024 and then only increasing slightly in 2025. Still, without the lower impairments, the bank’s profit margins would actually have decreased over the period.

The worsening asset utilization ties in with what we observed with the worsening NIM earlier. Comparing with Bank B though, Bank B’s profit margin is consistently below that of Bank A and is down from the levels it had in 2022. Both Banks have declining asset utilization but the impact on Bank A has been more significant. The worsening ROA is therefore due to the worsening asset efficiency for both banks, driven for Bank A by its declining operating income. Given that the bank’s assets are increasing consistently over time, but operating income is down, there may be some concerns around the current mix of the bank’s assets and whether it needs to change this mix to better generate revenue in future.

Moving to ROE, this has been declining for both banks, consistent with the decrease in ROA. This is despite the leverage for both banks increasing which would have increased ROE. This again illustrates what I mentioned in lectures where a small change in a small value can have a disproportionate impact on the overall equation. It would appear that both banks need to improve their asset efficiency while Bank B also appears to have had some recent issues with its profit margins (although there has been a marginal improvement in 2024). The leverage increasing is both a concern in terms of increasing risk, but perhaps also necessary as a way to improve ROE given the currently-low ROA.

3 marks per ratio discussed (5 x 3 = 15 marks) plus 3 additional marks for additional insightful commentary and structure/organisation.

questions.title: Question 3
questions.scenario: Twinkle Twinkle (Pty) Ltd. is a company headquartered in South Africa. It has mostly exhausted growth in the local market due to limited demand for its products as it struggles to compete with cheaper products from competitors. It therefore wishes to expand into new markets overseas and is also considering bringing in cheaper raw materials from international suppliers in order to help bring costs down and make it more competitive locally.

parts.required: 3.1 What would you consider to be the three biggest risks Twinkle will have to contend with if it plans to expand its supply chain overseas? Your answer should focus on both the supplier and customer side.
parts.memo:
Any of the three issues or something close would be fine (these are straight from the slides) – max 3 marks each.

Direct foreign exchange risks are now borne by the firm. Operating in multiple markets gives rise to forex risk due to the risk of volatility between foreign currencies. The current International Monetary System is a combination of floating and managed exchange rate policies. The variation in exchange rates affects the profitability of firms and all MNCs must understand foreign exchange risks in order to anticipate increased competition from imports or value-increasing opportunities from exports.

Political Risk now becomes a greater concern. Political risk is the risk of loss (or gain) from unforeseen government actions or other political events. MNCs must assess the political risk not only in countries where they currently operate but also where they expect to establish subsidiaries. This risk is often greater in emerging economies which can offer higher growth opportunities, potentially untapped markets and other benefits which need to be traded off against higher risks including political.

The evaluation of credit risk of foreign buyers and sellers is now key as reducing the possibility of non-payment for exports and non-delivery of imports is vital to the firm’s operations.

There are also market imperfections. There are significant differences among nations’ laws, tax systems, business practices and general cultural environments. Though there are risks and costs in coping with these market imperfections, they also offer managers of international firms’ opportunities

parts.required: 3.2 Twinkle does not have a large capex budget available and therefore would not be able to invest significantly into a new overseas operation. Provide two alternative options it has for selling its products overseas without having to make a significant investment abroad.
parts.memo:
Any of the following would be acceptable – the key being that they need to be options that do not require significant investment. 2 marks each.

Licensing: A firm in one country licenses the use of some or all of its intellectual property (patents, trademarks, copyrights, brand names) to a firm of some other country in exchange for fees or some royalty payment. Licensing enables a firm to use its technology in foreign markets without a substantial investment in those countries.

Franchising: A firm in one country authorising a firm in another country to utilise its brand names, logos etc. in return for royalty payments. This differs from licensing in that the franchisor typically also offers know-how and access to a business system.

Management contracts: A firm in one country agrees to operate facilities or provide other management services to a firm in another country for an agreed upon fee.

Joint ventures: A corporate entity or partnership that is jointly owned and operated by two or more firms is known as a joint venture. Joint ventures allow two firms to apply their respective comparative advantage in a given project.
